articles.title: Google dodges another breakup attempt
articles.summary: US District Court Judge Leonie Brinkema issued her remedies decision in the Justice Department’s ad tech antitrust trial against Google.
articles.body: US District Court Judge Leonie Brinkema declined the Justice Department’s request to make Google sell off parts of its ad tech business, accepting milder remedies to restore competition to markets it illegally monopolized for years. Brinkema said she would adopt most of the behavioral changes proposed by the parties, with some modifications. But those won’t become public until the parties meet to work out any additional proposed revisions and to review the judge’s opinion for confidential information that must be redacted. They could include proposals like restricting Google from using self-preferencing ad auction tactics or letting third-party ad tech tools access the same real-time information as Google. Once the final opinion comes out, Google can decide to appeal Brinkema’s underlying decision ruling it an illegal ad tech monopoly, as it recently did for a separate judgement that it had monopolized the online search market. In that case, Judge Amit Mehta also declined to go as far as a breakup, opting instead for Google to share data with competitors and alter its behavior. In the ad tech case, the DOJ successfully argued that Google had illegally monopolized the markets for publisher ad servers — where publishers can manage ad space for sale on their sites — and ad exchanges, which facilitate the auctions through which that ad space is sold. The judge agreed that Google had illegally tied its publisher ad server, Doubleclick for Publishers (DFP), and AdX ad exchange together in an anticompetitive manner that made it nearly impossible for customers to leave, degrading any competition. However, Brinkema found that the DOJ failed to prove Google illegally monopolized a market for advertiser-side tools. Ryan Pauley, president of The Verge’s parent company PMX Global, was deposed during the case. “We’re very pleased the Court rejected the DOJ’s proposal to break apart tools that help small businesses reach new customers and grow,” Google VP of regulatory affairs Lee-Anne Mulholland said in a statement. In a statement on X, the DOJ Antitrust Division said it was “pleased that the court ordered substantial relief” and that it was “evaluating appropriate next steps.” DOJ Associate AG Stanley Woodward Jr. added, “The timing of the Court’s order reflects the tradeoffs between immediate relief and remedies obtained through years of litigation.” Google has been the subject of antitrust backlash under both Democratic and Republican administrations. During the Biden administration, then-Sen. JD Vance (R-OH) said Federal Trade Commission Chair Lina Khan was “one of the few people in the Biden administration who I think is doing a pretty good job,” largely as a result of her scrutiny on tech. The remedies decision concludes the district court phase of the third major tech monopoly case brought by the federal government in recent years. Besides the two Google antitrust cases brought by the DOJ, the Federal Trade Commission brought a monopolization case against Meta, which it recently lost, and trials between federal enforcers and Amazon and Apple, respectively, are expected to take place in the coming years.

articles.title: Cybercrime losses near $21B: 5 ways to protect your money
articles.summary: The FBI reports nearly $21 billion in cybercrime losses for 2025, up 26%, as AI scams make fake voices and identities more convincing than ever.
articles.body: Nearly $21 billion. That number jumped out at me when I looked at the FBI's latest cybercrime data. Behind that enormous loss are families who watched savings disappear and people who trusted the wrong investment pitch. Some victims had no clue someone was moving their money until they checked an account. Americans reported nearly $21 billion in losses to cyber-enabled crime during 2025, up 26% from the year before. Investment fraud caused the biggest financial hit at about $8.65 billion. I recently joined "Fox & Friends Weekend" to talk about those numbers and a bigger problem I see coming. Scammers now have AI tools that can make a fake message, voice or identity far more believable than the clumsy scams many of us learned to recognize years ago. That changes how we need to protect our money. Here are five practical steps you can take now to put stronger barriers between scammers and your savings. Missed CyberGuy LIVE? Watch the Protect Your Money replay Our free CyberGuy LIVE class, Protect Your Money From Today’s Biggest Threats , has ended, but you can still watch the full replay and download our financial protection checklist. Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson walks you through five simple ways to help defend yourself against AI scams, fraud, identity theft and financial hacks. You’ll learn how to set up bank alerts, strengthen your account logins, protect your phone number, freeze your credit and help secure your retirement savings against unauthorized transfers. No technical experience is needed. Get the free replay and checklist now at CyberGuyLive.com IDENTITY THEFT LOSSES SURGE 70% FOR OLDER AMERICANS AI is helping scammers sound more convincing For years, one of the standard pieces of scam advice was to look for obvious mistakes. Maybe an email had terrible grammar. Perhaps the caller sounded suspicious. AI can now erase many of those clues. The FBI says its Internet Crime Complaint Center received 22,364 complaints in 2025 that included AI-related information. Reported losses tied to those complaints reached about $893 million. The FBI also warns that criminals can use AI to create fake social profiles, cloned voices and convincing videos. That gives scammers another way to build trust before asking for money or personal information. So telling you to "be careful" no longer feels like enough advice to me. I want barriers between a scammer and your money. 5 ways to protect your money from cybercrime You cannot predict every scam that may come your way. However, you can put safeguards in place that make it harder for a criminal to reach your money. 1) Turn on instant alerts for your financial accounts Start with your bank and credit cards. Open the official app or website for each financial institution and look for notification settings. Turn on alerts for transactions and transfers. You may also be able to receive warnings about suspicious account activity. The exact choices vary by bank. However, the goal stays simple. If money moves and you did not authorize it, you want to know quickly. I have talked with victims who discovered fraud long after criminals gained access. A real-time alert gives you a chance to call the financial institution and react much sooner. 2) Strengthen the login protecting your money Next, check the security settings on your bank, credit card and investment accounts. Use a strong password that you do not reuse elsewhere, which a password manager can help you create and store. Then turn on two-factor or multifactor authentication (2FA) wherever your financial institution offers it. If the company supports an authenticator app, passkey or another stronger verification method, consider using that option. Texted security codes still add protection, although your phone number can become a target in a SIM swap attack. Also protect the email account connected to your finances. A criminal who controls your email may be able to reset passwords or intercept account notifications. For a closer look at the different login options, see Are bank text codes enough to protect you? 3) Lock down your phone number Your phone number has quietly become part of your financial security. In a SIM swap or port-out scam, a criminal tricks a carrier into moving your number to another SIM or device. Once that happens, calls and texted security codes can start going to the scammer. Contact your carrier or check its account-security settings. Look for a number transfer lock, port-out protection or another feature designed to block unauthorized transfers. If your phone suddenly loses service for no clear reason, pay attention. Contact your carrier from another device, especially if you also notice unusual activity involving your financial accounts. IDENTITY RESTORATION: WHAT TO DO AFTER IDENTITY THEFT 4) Freeze your credit before a criminal uses it A credit freeze remains one of the strongest free tools available for preventing new-account fraud. You need to place a freeze separately with Equifax, Experian and TransUnion. Once active, the freeze restricts access to your credit file and makes it much harder for someone to open a new credit account using your identity. A freeze does not hurt your credit score. You can also lift it when you legitimately need to apply for credit. One warning: go directly to the official credit bureau websites rather than clicking an ad or unfamiliar search result. Criminals know people search for credit-freeze help too. CyberGuy has step-by-step guidance on how to freeze your credit and clean up your online data at Cyberguy.com 5) Give your retirement accounts more protection This one worries me because retirement accounts can represent decades of someone's work. We recently covered a case involving a Colgate-Palmolive employee whose entire $751,430 401(k) was allegedly drained after an impostor changed the account's contact information. The case later settled on undisclosed terms. Log in to your retirement and investment accounts and review their security settings. Make sure your contact information remains correct. Turn on account alerts and multifactor authentication. Then ask your brokerage or retirement-plan provider what protections it offers for withdrawals and transfers. Some providers offer additional verification or other controls that can make unauthorized transfers harder. This deserves the same attention you give your checking account. Maybe more. Missed CyberGuy LIVE? Watch the replay If you want to go deeper than the steps above, I will walk through each one in more detail in my CyberGuy LIVE class, Protect Your Money From Today's Biggest Threats . The live event has ended, but the full replay and CyberGuy Money Protection checklist are available now. In the class, I show you how to put these protections in place step by step, including where to look for bank alerts, how to strengthen account logins, ways to lock down your phone number, how to freeze your credit and what to ask your retirement or investment provider about added safeguards. You can pause the replay and work through each step at your own pace. Watch the free CyberGuy LIVE replay and get the Money Protection checklist at CyberGuyLive.com YOUR BANK MAY STOP TEXTING YOU SIX-DIGIT CODES Kurt's key takeaways What worries me about the FBI's nearly $21 billion figure goes beyond the size of the number. Scammers have become better at taking advantage of moments when people naturally trust what they see or hear. AI raises the stakes because a familiar voice or polished message can create a false sense of confidence. The FBI's numbers show how much money is already disappearing through cyber-enabled crime. I would rather see you build protections now than depend on spotting one tiny clue in the middle of a convincing scam. Turn on the alerts and secure the accounts holding your money. Then look at the protections surrounding your phone number, credit and retirement savings. Cybercriminals only need one good opportunity. Your job is to make that opportunity much harder to find. Have you ever received a scam call, email or investment pitch that was so convincing you almost believed it? What finally tipped you off? articles.title: Amazon, Walmart Face Data Requests in DOJ Beef Antitrust Probe
articles.summary: The US Justice Department expanded its antitrust inquiry of the meatpacking industry by demanding information on surging beef prices from eight major food re...
articles.body:
(Bloomberg) -- The US Justice Department expanded its antitrust inquiry of the meatpacking industry by demanding information on surging beef prices from eight major food retailers, including Amazon.com Inc., Costco Wholesale Corp. and Walmart Inc.

In a social media post Tuesday, DOJ said Associate Attorney General Stanley Woodward, the department's No. 3 official, sent letters last month seeking the price data from Amazon, Costco, Walmart, Albertsons Cos., Kroger Co., the US unit of Koninklijke Ahold Delhaize NV, Publix Super Markets Inc. and Aldi Inc.

In May, the Justice Department said it was examining potential antitrust violations in meatpacking. The agency normally conducts investigations privately, but President Donald Trump publicly requested the probe last year amid record beef prices. Woodward is overseeing antitrust enforcement at DOJ while the Senate considers Trump's nominee for the role.

Woodward, in letters dated July 14, asked the grocers to supply investigators with details about their beef purchasing and strategy, as well as retail pricing, profit margins and market analysis, for the past six years.

The grocers and the Justice Department didn't immediately respond to requests for comment.

Beef prices have repeatedly topped records, making it one of the biggest drivers of food inflation. Ground beef averaged $7.116 a pound in July, plateauing slightly but remaining near an all-time high, according to the US Bureau of Labor Statistics. Trump has tried to tamp down prices before the midterm elections in November, and most recently announced he would allow as much as 300,000 metric tons of imports at lower tariff rates over the next 90 days to boost supplies.

Walmart said in July that it would cut prices of seasonal products, including beef.

With assistance from Matt Day and Jaewon Kang.

articles.title: Rome declares security ‘red zone’ around the Colosseum to protect tourists amid violent crime incidents
articles.summary: Extra police and military deployed have been deployed to the Italian capital’s historic center to combat rising crime, drug dealing, and safety threats affecting tourists.
articles.body: Rome’s ancient Colosseum, where gladiators were once gored by wild animals to the delight of cheering crowds, has never exactly been associated with safety. Even in fiction, Henry James’ heroine “Daisy Miller” succumbed to malaria caught during a moonlight visit to the amphitheater. Today, the danger has a more modern twist. In July, a group of about 50 young people left police officers injured in an attack that involved shooting fireworks. Authorities say the incident was part of a pattern of increased crime around the historic area. In an effort to turn the tide on security issues at the Colosseum, Rome’s officials have now declared the area around the site a “red zone,” meaning that extra security has been deployed with greater powers to protect both residents and tourists, blaming the recent trouble on “predatory crimes and drug dealing” linked to urban decay. Imposed in late August, the zone will remain in place until December 24. Extra security has also been added near the city’s main Termini train station, St. Peter’s Basilica, and the Basilica of Santa Maria Maggiore, which has seen an increase in visitors since Pope Francis was laid to rest in a tomb there in April 2025. The new red zone will see local police presence enhanced around the clock alongside a military presence. Italy’s military already protects high-traffic tourist attractions with barriers and pop-up checkpoints. But armed officers dressed in camouflage alongside military vehicles have apparently not acted as enough of a deterrent to petty criminals. “Security is tight here, but I just saw a woman get pickpocketed,” Janelle Triton, an American tourist visiting the Colosseum site from Philadelphia, told CNN on Tuesday afternoon. She said the thief had gone by the time law enforcement was alerted. “We were told by our hotel not to come here at night though, so we have avoided the area.” The decline in safety at one of Rome’s most prestigious attractions comes despite millions of dollars spent on infrastructure improvements in recent years — investments which officials have admitted may actually be fueling crime. ‘Serious public emergency’ Lamberto Giannini, who’s responsible for security in Rome, says a new Colosseum metro station that was part of an $8.3 billion project to enhance the city’s underground subway system is one of the factors behind the rise in incidents. The station, which opened in December 2025, contains a multi-floor underground museum showcasing artifacts unearthed during years of construction work on a new metro line. But Giannini says it has also become a conduit for marginalized youth heading into Rome’s historical center to prey on both visitors and the residents who visit the area after the tourists have left. The red zone ordinance issued by Giannini states that existing security measures have proved inadequate in tackling a “serious public emergency” that presents a “risk of serious damage” to sensitive areas. It gives security officers greater powers to arrest suspected troublemakers or to order them to leave the area. A spokesperson for the prefect told CNN there would be no further comment on the issue, but a report in September is expected to detail what impact the red zone has had on crime.

images.caption: The view of the Colosseum in Rome, Italy, on October 7, 2025, still speaks to the grandeur and brutality of ancient Roman civilization and is among the world's top 10 most visited historical monuments.
The Colosseum is one of the most popular tourist attractions, and as such, it's also a target for criminals.

articles.title: Traveling for Labor Day? Here’s how to renew your TSA PreCheck
articles.summary: If you think it’s nearly time to renew your TSA PreCheck, here’s how to do it.
articles.body:
( NewsNation ) — The Transportation Security Administration (TSA) expects more than 17 million travelers to come through airports across the country for this upcoming Labor Day weekend.

While arriving at the airport early and being prepared can relieve some of the wait time in long security lines, some travelers opt for TSA PreCheck , which offers flyers a quicker airline security experience.

If you think it’s nearly time to renew your PreCheck , here’s how to do it.

TSA PreCheck offers flyers shorter wait times by eliminating such hassles as having to remove articles of clothing while in line or removing electronics and liquids from bags.

According to PreCheck provider Telos , most PreCheck passengers wait less than 10 minutes in dedicated security lines.

PreCheck is valid for five years at a time. You can renew up to six months before your TSA PreCheck expires.

TSA PreCheck can be renewed through three providers: Clear, Idemia and Telos. Renewal can be done online or in person.

You don’t need your passport or ID to renew your PreCheck online. You will need to know your nine-digit Known Traveler Number (KTN), which you can look up , as well as your date of birth and legal last name (legal name changes require an in-person visit). Any changes to your contact or address information should also be noted.

Renewal costs vary slightly by provider and whether it’s done online or in person, but travelers can expect to pay from $60 to $80. For providers Clear and Idemia, it is cheaper to renew online. For Telos, it is cheaper to renew in person.

In addition, some credit cards offer statement credit toward TSA PreCheck renewal fees.

articles.title: SEC investigating Daktronics in Kawhi Leonard case
articles.summary: The federal government and the NBA are investigating video display and scoreboard manufacturer Daktronics in connection with a scandal involving the Los Angeles Clippers in which the club allegedly circumvented the league’s salary cap to sign star player Kawhi Leonard. During Daktronics’s first-quarter earnings call, chief financial officer Howard Atkins confirmed the company had received requests…
articles.body:
The federal government and the NBA are investigating video display and scoreboard manufacturer Daktronics in connection with a scandal involving the Los Angeles Clippers in which the club allegedly circumvented the league’s salary cap to sign star player Kawhi Leonard.

During Daktronics’s first-quarter earnings call, chief financial officer Howard Atkins confirmed the company had received requests for information from the NBA and the Securities and Exchange Commission “seeking information from us concerning the company and Mr. Leonard.”

“We take these requests seriously and are cooperating,” Atkins said, according to Dallas Business Journal . “At this point, out of respect for the respective processes, we will not be providing further comment.”

Daktronics is at the center of a story published earlier this year by independent sports journalist Pablo Torre laying out how Leonard was allegedly paid millions by the company using money from the Clippers, which have a video board designed by Daktronics in their arena.

The Clippers signed Leonard to a three-year extension worth nearly $150 million in 2024.

Torre first reported on the Clippers and billionaire owner Steve Ballmer’s efforts to circumvent the NBA salary cap last fall, with the club denying the allegations and arguing it was defrauded by investors.

ESPN reported last month the NBA has no evidence to suggest Ballmer funneled money through team sponsors to pay Leonard directly, but rather, the league is focused on “whether the team’s introduction of Leonard to team sponsors constitutes a violation of the league’s rules prohibiting salary cap circumvention.”

articles.title: Big tech is investing millions in data centers and saving a quick tax buck while doing it—leaving some states collecting revenue loss
articles.summary: 36 out of the 50 states in the country employ tax incentives for data center development, allowing the projects to save on equipment costs.
articles.body:
It's no secret AI giants are racing against each other to build data centers across the country. With the AI boom skyrocketing in the 2020s, the U.S. has grown to nearly 5,000 data centers across all 50 states to date, with hyperscalers driving much of that expansion. But with that growth comes tax incentives that seem to scale further than market competition.

According to a report from JLL, a commercial real estate and investment management company, the global data center sector will likely expand at a 14% compound annual growth rate through 2030—and it notes "hyperscalers will remain a key driver of sector growth." And with that growth comes significant savings for the hyperscalers: nearly three-quarters of all states employ tax incentives for data center development—which include exemptions from sales and use tax, property tax and "financial transactions" tax.

The eligibility of these exemptions differ state by state, however. Some states like Texas require a substantial—at least $200 million—capital investment in the data center project, others such as Maine require a certain amount of square footage to be eligible, and a few states also require employment metrics to be met. Certain states, like New York, have no minimum investment requirement—and to sweeten the deal further, the tax exemptions are applicable for a wide range of data center expenditures.

Such measures are evident in the New York Department of Taxation and Finance structure, for example, in which data center tax incentive eligibility covers property, services, equipment and contracts. The incentives for the data centers themselves lie in the inherent replacement cycle required for upgrades and system life.

Capital expenditures like electrical systems, batteries and structures have usable lives in excess of 20 years—but other types of equipment such as cloud computing operations often have lives of as short as three years due to the high strain of AI computing. Based on the nature of equipment churn, the Tax Foundation found that a $5 billion data center could "easily spend more than a billion dollars a year on machinery and equipment," making sales taxation a "significant" consideration when choosing development.

Data centers, assuming they meet the minimum threshold required to be eligible depending on the state, are exempt from paying sales tax on equipment and machinery for years following their construction. States that already do not employ sales tax, such as New Jersey, incentivize data center development through property tax abatements and tax credits instead. This effectively means states are passing up billions in tax revenue to further cultivate the AI boom.

images.caption: Thousands of data centers have been constructed across the country, and states have lost billions in tax revenue for it. · Fortune · Pete Kiehart/Bloomberg via Getty Images

articles.title: It sure looks like hackers breached a major ID card verification service | TechCrunch
articles.summary: An identity theft search site claimed to have more than 150 million driver's license photos stolen from an ID verification service. The crime site has now shut down.
articles.body:
If you have handed over your driver’s license, passport, or other form of identity document to verify your information in the real world, like at a bar, a weed store, or when booking a car rental, there’s a good chance it’s now been stolen in a suspected massive data breach.

That’s according to a jaw-dropping report by independent security journalist Brian Krebs, who says a company used to verify government-issued identity documents in the real world was likely hacked and its vast stores of people’s ID cards were exfiltrated.

Krebs reports that an identity theft site called Nexus, which launched on the dark web this week, claimed to allow users to search through more than 150 million driver’s licenses and passports belonging to people who live in the United States and Canada. A post advertising the site on a known Russian cybercrime forum said Nexus added about half a million new documents daily, sourced from a “major identity verification company,” implying that the hackers had near real-time access to the identity verification company’s systems.

The advert claims that “customer photos are displayed if available.” Krebs found that his own driver’s license was among the searchable records in the database, confirming that the data was authentic. Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth was also among the people whose photos were listed on the identity search site.

A spokesperson for the Department of Defense told TechCrunch that it is “aware of these reports and is evaluating them.”

Working with security researcher Zach Edwards , whose ID card was also stolen in the breach, Krebs identified the likely source as the identity verification service IDScan . The Louisiana-based company is relied on by major tech and consumer brands to verify tens of millions of people’s IDs around the world each month.

IDScan chief executive Jimmy Roussel did not return TechCrunch’s request for comment, but the company’s chief operating officer Jillian Kossman told Krebs that the company was investigating. Krebs said the FBI’s field office in New Orleans is also probing the breach. A spokesperson for the FBI did not respond to TechCrunch’s inquiry about the breach.

Nexus went offline shortly after Krebs’ report went live.

This data breach comes as governments are increasingly rolling out age-verification laws , which largely rely on requiring adults to upload their identity documents to verify that they are old enough to enter a website or app. Security experts and privacy advocates have long warned that companies storing vast amounts of people’s identity documents for long periods of time put that data at risk of theft by hackers.

By all accounts, this would be the largest known single breach of identity documents in some time.

articles.title: Lutnick claims that data centers, known for water consumption, ‘don’t use water’
articles.summary: Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick claimed Wednesday that data centers “don’t use water” despite the facilities’ significant water usage raising concerns for communities that may host them. In an interview with CNBC, Lutnick said, “One of my favorite things is when people talk about data centers using water. The No. 1 product in America that uses…
articles.body:
Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick claimed Wednesday that data centers “don’t use water” despite the facilities’ significant water usage raising concerns for communities that may host them.

In an interview with CNBC , Lutnick said, “One of my favorite things is when people talk about data centers using water. The No. 1 product in America that uses water is cattle.”

“I mean, data centers don’t use water,” he added. “This is propaganda by our adversaries to try to slow us down.”

Data centers used an estimated 66 billion liters of water in 2023, most of which went to hyperscale data centers, according to a 2024 report from the Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory. Hyperscalers alone are expected to consume between 60 billion and 124 billion liters in 2028, the report projected.

In 2015, the total U.S. water use was estimated to be about 322 billion gallons per day, or more than 400 trillion liters per year. At that time, the government estimated that power plants were the nation’s largest water users, followed by irrigation.

AI companies have argued that concerns over data center water usage are overblown, pointing to other industries that use more water. However, even industry trade groups acknowledge that data centers use some quantity of water.

They have also sought to underscore new technologies, such as closed-loop cooling systems, that can limit the amount of water new data centers require.

Lutnick’s comments come as the Trump administration has repeatedly defended data centers despite growing bipartisan backlash against the AI infrastructure. President Trump on Monday called on the U.S. to “let Data reign” and accused data center opponents of wanting their communities to be “backwards and poor.”

“The good news is that there are plenty of other places that want them. If we kill the Golden Goose, you will only have yourselves to blame. China could not be happier with this anti Data Center movement,” Trump wrote on Truth Social .

Water use is just one factor behind the public pushback to the server warehouses. Americans have also raised concerns about high electric bills, noise and pollution.

The House Energy and Commerce Committee is expected to hold a hearing Thursday on draft legislation to address data centers’ water usage.

articles.title: G20 wraps without consensus amid bond market sell-off
articles.summary: The US-hosted G20 meeting, beset by trade and diplomatic squabbles, wrapped up after failing to ease investors’ concerns over a global bond market sell-off.
articles.body:
The US-hosted G20 meeting, beset by trade and diplomatic squabbles, wrapped Tuesday after failing to ease investors' concerns over a global bond market sell-off.

As global bond yields hit multi-decade highs , the gathering of finance ministers ended without a consensus after China objected to language used in the communiqué about eliminating "non-market policies" driving global imbalances. The Europeans, meanwhile, refused to take the "family photo" with their Russian counterpart, whose presence galled US allies already put out by the Iran conflict, along with Washington's trade war and bond market interventions.

For anyone hoping the G20 summit "suggested an end to the deficits, inflation and geopolitical disruptions… roiling investors," The Wall Street Journal's chief economics commentator wrote, " you've been disappointed ."

articles.title: Trump under pressure to contain Iran fighting as midterms near
articles.summary: President Trump is under pressure to avoid an escalatory spiral after launching the largest wave of strikes on Iran in weeks, with the U.S. military strained and the midterm elections rapidly approaching. Trump on Wednesday downplayed the Iran war’s negative impact on Republican candidates. The president’s approval rating has reached a record low — 33…
articles.body:
President Trump is under pressure to avoid an escalatory spiral after launching the largest wave of strikes on Iran in weeks, with the U.S. military strained and the midterm elections rapidly approaching.

Trump on Wednesday downplayed the Iran war’s negative impact on Republican candidates. The president’s approval rating has reached a record low — 33 percent — and two-thirds have a negative view of his handling of the war. Brent crude ticked up on Wednesday, with oil prices surpassing $90 a barrel.

“I don’t think it will be very much longer,” Trump said, responding to a question of what more Iranian targets the U.S. can hit, as the war drags on past the six-month mark.

“And I’m not affected by the election. Number one, I’m not running, but my party’s running, and I’m going to help my party. But I think my party respects the fact that we’re not allowing Iran to have a nuclear weapon.”

However, Reuters reported that the White House is looking to avoid ramping up military action against Iran until after the Nov. 3 election.

Trump, in a Truth Social post Tuesday, warned Iran against further strikes, claiming the U.S. was “justified.” American allies across the Middle East that host U.S. bases came under fire overnight Tuesday, with Bahrain, Iraq, Jordan and Kuwait all reporting Iranian attacks.

The back-and-forth military strikes this week marked the largest outbreak in fighting after a month of relative calm. On Tuesday, U.S. forces carried out approximately 100 strikes against Iranian targets in what they said was retaliation for maritime threats near the Strait of Hormuz.

Iranian state media said a U.S. strike hit a home in southern Iran where a wedding celebration was taking place , killing two women and two children and injuring 60 others.

Mona Yacoubian, director and senior adviser of the Middle East Program at the Center for Strategic and International Studies (CSIS), said the latest escalation “falls well within the pattern of the conflict over the past several months: unstable lulls of no-war/no-peace eventually collapse into a renewal of tit-for-tat strikes, but as long as neither side is interested in a return to all-out war, we will likely continue to see this type of low level conflict.”

“This is not a turning point in the conflict, and Trump is not ‘mowing the lawn’ which would be a strategy to pursue post-conflict — a return to occasional strikes as needed to keep Iran off balance,” she said. “We’re still very much in the conflict.”

The U.S. said this week’s strikes were a preemptive response to Iran attempting to launch rockets with sea mines into the Strait of Hormuz. And the U.S. reportedly hit two Iranian tankers in the first direct retaliation for strikes on tankers in the strait, with Axios reporting the administration describing it as a “tanker-for-tanker” policy.

Behnam Ben Taleblu, a senior fellow at the Foundation for Defense of Democracies, said the Trump administration “is adopting a very militarized form of containment, which is actually not a bad option given the preferred approach … which is economic pressure, economic coercion.”

“I think the Trump administration is comfortable with this militarized form of containment, I think it actually has a winning approach to try to back end this regime and present it with a series of hybrid crises, and to see where is it that the regime will buckle, where is it that the regime will break, where is it that the regime will bend, where is it the regime will double down, and then strike at those weak points,” he added.

The traffic in the strait dropped by 50 percent on Monday, with only five successful ship crossings compared to 10 passages each day over the weekend, according to ship-tracking firm Kpler.

Tehran is sending mixed messages on whether it is seeking to escalate or pursue diplomacy.

Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian called for the U.S. to return to commitments of the memorandum of understanding (MOU) signed by both sides in mid-June, which was meant to impose a ceasefire, open the strait and set up talks about Iran’s nuclear program.

Trump and Secretary of State Marco Rubio have dismissed that possibility out of hand.

“That ship, in many ways, has sailed,” Rubio said in the interview on “The Brian Kilmeade Show” — arguing the Iranian regime has failed to engage in talks over its nuclear program.

“The core issue here is they’re never going to have a nuclear weapon,” he said. “And as long as they continue to endeavor or claim to want one, they’re going to pay a price for it, and that price is going to be primarily economic. But we reserve the right, as we said, to take military action when necessary — not just to protect ourselves but to prevent them from being able to threaten others as well.”

Yacoubian said a return to the MOU isn’t viable for the U.S. or Iran since the two countries “remain quite far apart on core issues.”

“The level of distrust between the two sides has only grown over the intervening months, making a return to negotiations all the more difficult,” she said. “The MOU as it was signed in mid-June largely favored Iran, so a return to the MOU would maintain several points in Iran’s favor.”

Meanwhile Mohsen Rezaei, the Iranian Supreme National Security Council secretary, warned on Wednesday that the U.S. will “fail to climb out of the infernal depths you have created for yourselves” in the face of a new Iranian “strategy on the battlefield, in diplomacy, and in countering the economic siege”.

Other than the recent rounds of strikes, the U.S. military is continuing to enforce the naval blockade in the Arabian Sea, barring ships from entering or departing Iranian ports. So far, the U.S. forces have redirected 86 commercial vessels, disabled three and boarded another two to ensure compliance, the U.S. Central Command said in an update on Wednesday.

The prolonged war with Iran is also putting a strain on the U.S. military’s stockpile of premium munitions such as long-range missiles and interceptors, undermining the president’s leverage over Iran and prompting worries among some defense officials and lawmakers on Capitol Hill .

The U.S. military has used up nearly all army tactical missile systems and precision strike missiles, along with the majority of its Terminal High Altitude Area Defense interceptors.

The U.S. forces had between 759 and 827 Patriot interceptors as of late July, a recent estimate from CSIS said, far below the more than 2,300 the military had before the Iran war started in late February.

Ben Taleblu said the strain on U.S. munitions explains, in some part, the “piecemeal approach Washington is taking.”

“It affects the actual targets, the number of strikes, the willingness to get into a more protracted spiral with the Iranians,” he said.

articles.title: NBA docks Clippers 5 first round picks, $30M for Kawhi Leonard scandal
articles.summary: The NBA on Wednesday announced sweeping sanctions against the Los Angeles Clippers for what the league said was an intentional effort to circumvent its salary cap by funneling money to star player Kawhi Leonard through endorsement opportunities and other income in order to sign him in 2024. The Clippers initiated “off-court income opportunities” between Leonard…
articles.body:
The NBA on Wednesday announced sweeping sanctions against the Los Angeles Clippers for what the league said was an intentional effort to circumvent its salary cap by funneling money to star player Kawhi Leonard through endorsement opportunities and other income in order to sign him in 2024.

The Clippers initiated “off-court income opportunities” between Leonard and four companies doing business with the team: Aspiration Partners, Boingo Wireless, Daktronics and Lockton Insurance, NBA investigators found.

The team facilitated endorsement agreements between these companies by offering them business from the team and failed to report the income to the league.

“The NBA’s collectively bargained system for determining player compensation is a fundamental component of the basketball competition that the league oversees for the benefit of the teams and players and ultimately the fans,” commissioner Adam Silver said in a statement. “I am deeply disappointed by the flagrant violations of our rules and by the Clippers’ institutional and leadership failures that led to this misconduct. The severity of the penalties reflects the seriousness of the violations.”

The Clippers will lose five first round draft picks starting in 2029 and will be fined $30 million as part of the club’s punishment, while its owner Steve Ballmer has been suspended “from all league and team activities for one year for knowingly seeking to help Mr. Leonard obtain off-court income opportunities, for approving a business deal that he knew was a precondition for Aspiration to enter into an endorsement agreement with Mr. Leonard, and for his failure to create conditions under which his organization abided by the NBA’s circumvention rules.”

News of the Clippers scandal was first reported last year by the independent journalist Pablo Torre, while one of the companies that allegedly did business with Leonard told its investors this week it was cooperating with officials from the NBA and the Securities and Exchange Commission.

It was unclear as of Wednesday if the Clippers, Ballmer, Leonard or the companies involved had violated any federal or state laws as part of the scheme to circumvent the salary cap.

In a statement to ESPN issued through his agent, Leonard said, “I accept full responsibility for lapses in judgment by people within my inner circle and regret the distraction this situation has caused the fans and my family.”

The Clippers, in a statement of their own to the outlet said they “vehemently reject the NBA’s findings,” which the Clippers called “the result of a heavily biased investigation seeking to justify a predetermined narrative rather than facts and evidence.”

articles.title: Toilet paper becomes a kitchen table issue for Trump again as Canada’s retaliatory tariffs could spell another shortage
articles.summary: A tariff fight with Canada is pushing tissue prices higher, echoing the shortage scare that preceded his 2020 election loss.
articles.body:
It seems like so long ago, but in the not-so-distant past, all of us were roaming the supermarket aisles for the last roll of TP , cursing at those who began stockpiling the rolls, and blaming the relative who brought a bidet back from Japan for not bringing one back for you as well. While the days of reaching for the last TP under a "limit one roll per customer" sign shoddily taped to the rack may be over, the thought of a shortage possibly returning to haunt the same president six years later isn't far-fetched.

After trade talks between the U.S. and Canada broke down in late August, Washington imposed a 50% tariff on roughly $20 billion of Canadian goods under a section of the Tariff Act of 1930—a Depression-era law that lets the president retaliate against countries seen as discriminating against U.S. commerce. In response, Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney vowed to match the US "dollar for dollar," and unveiled retaliatory tariffs on close to 900 American products, set to take effect next week, on Sept. 8. Chief among them? Toilet paper and paper products.

"Canada will match those tariffs dollar for dollar," Carney said two weeks ago. "Because we were attacked. Like, you're at war when you get attacked."

Paper goods are among the hardest hit. Canada's retaliation puts a 25% duty on U.S. toilet paper and facial tissue, and a 50% duty on paper towels, napkins, and raw wood pulp. Canada is also charging 50% on American dairy products (except cheese, which gets 25%) and 25% on American fish and seafood, including frozen lobster. It's in response to U.S. tariffs, including a 25% tariff on Canadian cars and auto parts—and Trump is now threatening to double that to 50% if no deal is reached by Jan. 1, 2027.

On March 12, 2020, U.S. toilet paper sales surged 734% compared with the same day the year before, making it the top-selling grocery item that day. By the time the panic subsided, roughly 70% of the world's grocery stores had run out of toilet paper at some point . Shelves that normally held Charmin and Cottonelle sat bare for weeks as retailers imposed purchase limits, and bamboo-paper startups saw Amazon sales jump more than 5,000% month over month as shoppers hunted for anything they could find. Researchers who studied the episode afterward found no actual break in production. Mills kept running. Hoarding, not a supply failure, created nearly all of it.

Eight months later, due to a confluence of the COVID-19 pandemic and his administration's handling of the virus, President Donald Trump lost the presidency to Joe Biden. Toilet paper didn't decide that election, but it became a small symbol of an economy that felt like it was slipping out of a president's control, just as voters decided whether to give him another term.

articles.title: CDC, Pennsylvania’s growing feud over measles: 4 things to know
articles.summary: Pennsylvania health officials last week announced two unvaccinated people died from measles-associated conditions, including an infant. But the announcement was just the beginning of a growing political controversy that’s pitting the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) against the state’s health department. The agency is publicly questioning Pennsylvania’s findings and has not yet counted the…
articles.body:
Pennsylvania health officials last week announced two unvaccinated people died from measles-associated conditions, including an infant.

But the announcement was just the beginning of a growing political controversy that’s pitting the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) against the state’s health department.

The agency is publicly questioning Pennsylvania’s findings and has not yet counted the two in its national tally of measles deaths.

Here are four things to know about the clash.

Last week, the Pennsylvania Department of Health recorded the first measles deaths in 35 years.

Both people were unvaccinated, they lived in Lancaster County and the state described the deaths as “measles-associated.” But that was all the information shared initially.

When pressed for more details at a press conference, including for the ages of the victims, Gov. Josh Shapiro (D) and the state’s secretary of health Dr. Debra Bogen declined to elaborate, citing patient confidentiality. All they would say is the deaths were “measles-associated.”

Shapiro, who is widely expected to run for president in 2028, said he had spoken to Health and Human Services (HHS) Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. and “made very clear that his actions and the rhetoric coming from this administration are having a negative impact on communities across America, particularly right here in Pennsylvania.”

The governor’s remarks set off a war of words between federal, state and local officials, including Kennedy, Shapiro, the Lancaster County coroner and county commissioners.

Anti-vaccine activists and Trump administration officials questioned whether the people had died from measles, or whether they happened to have measles but died from something else.

Some suggested health officials were using the phrase “measles-associated” to obfuscate the fact that the virus did not play a role in the reported deaths.

“They cannot find any measles deaths in Lancaster County,” Kennedy said the next day during an event in Florida. “The press is all covering this as if those measles deaths actually happened, but nobody is doing a little bit of critical inquiry to find out. We’re trying to figure out who those deaths were and whether they actually happened.”

According to the Pennsylvania Department of Health, the phrase is used when measles is present, but the disease may not be assessed by the medical certifier or coroner to be the immediate cause of death.

But none of that was discussed during Shapiro’s press conference, or in the initial statement from the state Health Department.

The CDC even released a statement applauding Kennedy’s “efforts to clarify conflicting information from Pennsylvania officials about whether the two reported deaths were caused by measles.”

Poor communication let misinformation flourish

The lack of initial details, seemingly contradictory statements from different officials and a vague phrase like “measles-associated” created an information vacuum that Kennedy and others quickly filled with misinformation.

Before any information was released, Ginger Taylor, who was recently appointed to serve on a federal autism research panel and has suggested there is a link between vaccines and autism, posted an image of a fake news headline claiming that the two patients were men in their 80s.

Public health experts said Pennsylvania officials also gave a masterclass in how not to communicate.

Amesh Adalja, an infectious disease physician at Johns Hopkins University Center for Health Security, said Shapiro shouldn’t have been the one giving a press conference.

“Since the very announcement of these deaths, this has been run like a political operation rather than a public health operation, and these are the results you get,” Adalja said.

Instead of defining the terms being used and emphasizing that there are open questions and an ongoing investigation into the cases, Shapiro attacked Kennedy.

“They operated it like a political operation, and they got burned,” Adalja said. “They hid behind statutes and refused to release information, and that created an information vacuum. They didn’t explain definitions, and it left them completely open for RFK Jr. to swoop in, and he did. And now there’s no way to really reverse all of this.”

After Shapiro’s press conference, details of the cases eventually began emerging, including that one of the deceased was an infant.

Then, the county coroner said the infant died due to a lacerated spleen and bleeding, not measles. He also said initially that his office had been notified of only one death, though Pennsylvania clarified that not all deaths must be reported to a coroner’s office.

He later changed his finding, saying measles was a “contributing factor” that was listed on the death certificate.

Kennedy revives ‘died from’ vs. ‘died with’ claims

Experts said when tracking an outbreak, there isn’t much of a distinction between whether someone died from measles or died with measles.

Having a measles infection when you die counts as a “measles-associated death” in Pennsylvania.

But the discourse is a common tactic among anti-vaccine activists. It was deployed during the COVID-19 pandemic to downplay the virus.

“They’re trying to play a word game to try to minimize the importance of measles,” said Demetre Daskalakis, the former director of the CDC National Center for Immunization and Respiratory Diseases.

“Kennedy and others are trying to take advantage of semantics, I think to try to create doubt around the importance of measles as a vaccine preventable disease,” Daskalakis said.

An example, Daskalakis explained, is if somebody who had underlying diabetes died of a heart attack. The heart attack was the immediate cause of death, but diabetes was the underlying reason for the heart disease and contributed to the death.

Critics say new CDC director failed her first major test

Dr. Erica Schwartz took charge of the agency last month amid a pledge to operate independently from Kennedy.

But in her first agency-wide meeting , Schwartz told agency staff that while she wouldn’t hesitate to disagree with Kennedy if necessary, she would not do so publicly.

During her confirmation hearing, several senators raised concerns that Schwartz would not stand up to the Health secretary.

Former officials and public health experts say those concerns have been validated, since the agency is now openly questioning Pennsylvania’s reporting of measles deaths.

Daskalakis said he is disappointed but not surprised.

“At the end of the day, I think that Dr. Schwartz has some really airtight credentials. Really sounds like a brilliant public health person. But I think being the CDC director role is not about appeasing your secretary; it’s about serving the people,” he said.

Adalja said the latest development is just more evidence that public health is being politicized, and the CDC can’t be trusted.

“I didn’t really have any high hopes for [Schwartz], and this just proves it,” Adalja said. “The CDC is a compromised organization. Its best people quit, or retired, or were fired. I think the CDC has been irreparably damaged by design by RFK Jr.”

articles.title: Hegseth headed for clash with GOP senators as frustrations grow
articles.summary: Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth is on a collision course with GOP senators as key lawmakers have major concerns about the turnover of senior staff, the lack of a clear plan for ending the Iran war, and the failure of the administration to reach out to Democrats to build support for funding priorities. Hegseth has…
articles.body:
Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth is on a collision course with GOP senators as key lawmakers have major concerns about the turnover of senior staff, the lack of a clear plan for ending the Iran war, and the failure of the administration to reach out to Democrats to build support for funding priorities.

Hegseth has been a controversial figure throughout his leadership of the Pentagon, but the growing tensions between him and senior GOP lawmakers will come to a head this fall when the administration makes a push for more than $70 billion in emergency national security spending to cover the growing costs of the Iran war.

Senate Republicans will demand more information about the departures of senior military officials, such as Secretary of the Army Dan Driscoll, who resigned this week, and about the conduct of the military conflict with Iran, which has now stretched for more than six months.

Sen. Thom Tillis (R-N.C.), a former member of the Senate Armed Services Committee, on Wednesday accused Hegseth of “inept management” of the Pentagon and called on President Trump to fire him.

“I have never witnessed more inept management of the brave men and women who serve our country. He is intimidated by competence and retreats to ginning up culture wars instead of soberly attending to the vital work of our national defense and the health and well-being of our fighting force,” Tillis posted on social platform X.

Tillis urged Trump “to find a new leader at the Pentagon who will retain and empower our military talent rather than diminish it.”

The Defense Department declined to respond to Tillis’s comments.

GOP senators have grown increasingly concerned over the forced departures of several experienced and well-respected senior military officials, such as Gen. Randy George, former Army chief of staff, and Gen. Christopher Donahue, the top Army commander in Europe, during Hegseth’s tenure.

Sen. Mike Rounds (R-S.D.), a senior member of the Senate Armed Services Committee, said he was “disappointed” to learn of Driscoll’s resignation.

“I was disappointed. I think he’s been a pretty solid guy. So disappointed,” he said.

Rounds said Driscoll was “frustrated with some of his top generals being released.”

“That’s not the first time I’ve heard that. I think that points to questions we’re going to be asking when we get back in terms of where’s the leadership at,” Rounds said.

“We’ve had some very good generals that are no longer there that we respected and that had a huge amount of foundational knowledge in terms of moving us forward as far as the changing capabilities that we need to incorporate into the overall fighting force,” he said.

A former senior Republican Armed Services staffer said many GOP lawmakers want to see a shake-up at the Pentagon and view Hegseth as a political liability heading into the Nov. 3 election but are leery about confronting Trump over a prominent member of his Cabinet.

“Hegseth has treated the Pentagon like his own personal playground in the culture wars. He’s driven out over two dozen senior leaders, including Driscoll, and ignored the chain of command by intervening personally in official investigations,” the former GOP aide said.

The former staffer said Hegseth is “an absolute train wreck for Republicans headed into the midterms but they are too scared to do anything about it,” noting they are relying on Trump to turn out voters and spend big on behalf of GOP candidates.

“If they had a spine, instead of wringing their hands and holding closed-door hearings, the leaders of the House and Senate Armed Services committees would say on the record what just about every voter knows, which is that Hegseth is unqualified for the job and never should have accepted the position when President Trump offered it to him,” the source added.

Asked if he still has confidence in Hegseth’s leadership, Rounds said “it’s a matter of whether the president” is confident in his secretary of Defense.

“The president chooses who he wants for his key leaders. I think they’re trying. We want to see results,” he said.

House Armed Services Committee Chair Mike Rogers (R-Ala.) told reporters Tuesday that he’s concerned about the turmoil among the senior ranks.

“I’m tired of all the churn. I want to see some stability,” he said.

Several of the departed generals who are highly regarded by GOP lawmakers, including George and Donahue, clashed with Hegseth over the creation of a special Unmanned Assault Battalion in Europe to study new drone-intensive tactics developed during the four-year war in Ukraine.

Gen. Christopher LaNeve, the acting Army chief of staff, ordered the battalion last month to refocus on its core mission as an airborne infantry battalion.

Both Tillis and Rounds questioned the decision to phase out the intensive program to experiment in drone warfare, which some GOP lawmakers view as the future of military conflict.

“Our understanding and assumptions of warfare are being challenged in places like Ukraine and Iran, and Dan [Driscoll] understands the old way of doing business no longer applies. He and General George began a transformative period of innovation in how we array our forces and equip our soldiers,” Tillis said.

Some Republicans warn the turnover of senior officials raises broader questions about the management of the Defense Department at a time the United States is mired in a conflict with Iran that has stretched far beyond the four or five weeks that Trump initially projected.

One Republican senator told The Hill in July that Hegseth was losing support within senior military ranks, which has, in turn, raised red flags for some GOP policymakers on Capitol Hill.

“I have heard out of the Pentagon that there’s a loss of confidence — within the Pentagon. And of course then everyone here on the Hill hears those same concerns,” the senator said, requesting anonymity to discuss private conversations with colleagues.

A big question on Capitol Hill is whether the Pentagon can continue to wage the conflict with Iran with any intensity if Congress doesn’t pass emergency defense funding before the end of September.

The extended deployment of Navy carriers, such as the USS Abraham Lincoln, which was at sea for 260 days before docking at port in Thailand on Wednesday, and the lack of transparency over military resources will be other subjects of inquiry this month.

Rounds and other Senate Republicans have questioned Hegseth’s approach of doing a lot of outreach to Republican lawmakers to build support for more than $70 billion in emergency defense funding while largely ignoring Democrats.

Rounds said he’s “frustrated” that Hegseth’s team hasn’t done more to build support for defense funding priorities across the aisle.

“They were only advising and working with Republicans. It needs to be both Republicans and Democrats at the table,” he said. “I think the administration needs to change its focus and they need to bring this back to a bipartisan effort with regard to the defense of our country.”

images.caption: Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth answers questions during a Senate Appropriations Committee hearing to review of the President’s supplemental funding request on July 21, 2026.

articles.title: Trump, AI industry go on offensive to counter data center backlash
articles.summary: President Trump and the AI industry are going on the offensive, attempting to bolster support for data centers as they contend with a groundswell of public opposition that has swept across party lines. Trump has not shied away from embracing the controversial server warehouses behind the AI boom, but he appeared to take a no-holds-barred approach Monday as he called for the U.S. to “let Data Reign” and accused the opposition of wanting…
articles.body:
President Trump and the AI industry are going on the offensive, attempting to bolster support for data centers as they contend with a groundswell of public opposition that has swept across party lines.

Trump has not shied away from embracing the controversial server warehouses behind the AI boom, but he appeared to take a no-holds-barred approach Monday as he called for the U.S. to “let Data Reign” and accused the opposition of wanting to be “ backwards and poor .”

The AI advocacy group Build American AI also launched a multimillion-dollar campaign Monday aimed at building support for “commonsense” data center policies, while a group of data center developers unveiled their own nonprofit Wednesday seeking to highlight benefits from the AI infrastructure.

The latest push comes as the data center buildout has increasingly become politically “toxic,” said Brendan Steinhauser, a GOP strategist and head of the advocacy group Alliance for Secure AI.

“The AI industry is losing and has been [losing] on this issue pretty much all year,” he told The Hill, adding, “The American people are skeptical of AI, skeptical of Big Tech, and the companies are trying to reverse that trend and it’s going to be very difficult.”

Nearly two-thirds of Americans — 63 percent — say they would oppose a new data center being built in their community, according to an Economist/YouGov poll released Tuesday. Another 51 percent say data centers are bad for the country.

This includes a sizeable share of Republicans, with 52 percent in the poll opposing nearby data center construction and 39 percent deeming the infrastructure bad for the U.S.

Trump finds himself “caught between this massive movement by his base that is skeptical of data centers and AI and the moneyed interests in Big Tech that are funding a lot of candidates and funding the party and even White House projects,” Steinhauser said.

The president has long embraced the AI buildout, keeping up the drumbeat for data centers even as public opinion soured and other GOP politicians tried to distance themselves from such projects.

When Texas Gov. Greg Abbott (R) announced a temporary data center moratorium last month, Trump called it a “mistake.” But he left room for Republicans to maneuver ahead of the midterms , where the AI infrastructure has increasingly become a central issue.

In key swing state races from Michigan to Pennsylvania to Wisconsin, GOP candidates have called to halt construction or accused their Democratic opponents of being overly cozy with AI companies.

“If Republicans are against a data center, that’s OK with me,” Trump said last month. “I’m only saying that if I ran a community … if I was a mayor or if I was a governor in the state, I would want to have the data centers because they bring tremendous income.”

However, the president took a different tack Monday, offering a sharp rebuke of data center opponents.

“The only reason that communities throughout the U.S.A. should not want Data Centers is if they want to end up being backwards and poor,” he wrote on Truth Social. “If they want to be successful and rich, with far lower taxes and jobs all over the place, let Data Reign.”

His comments faced pushback from a handful of lawmakers in his own party. Rep. Tim Burchett (R-Tenn.) responded by saying, “I guess I’m backwards and poor,” while Rep. Thomas Massie (R-Ky.) — a frequent Trump critic — said he doesn’t think “you should let data reign without any kind of regulation at the local level.”

Cooper Teboe, a Democratic strategist based in Silicon Valley, suggested Trump is “out of touch” and “genuinely seems to not understand why these things are such an issue with voters.”

“If you want to go all in on a 90-10 issue, 60 days before the midterms, I wish you luck and Godspeed,” he told The Hill, referring to an issue that has 90 percent opposition.

White House spokesperson Davis Ingle argued in a statement Wednesday that Trump’s “bold leadership is turning data centers into engines of growth and opportunity for communities across the country that want them.”

“By requiring data centers to pay for their own power, water, and utilities, the President has ensured the American people never foot the bill for private companies’ profits,” he added. “President Trump will continue leveraging the data center boom to deliver real benefits for working families and small businesses.”

The AI industry is simultaneously ramping up a charm offensive on data centers.

Build American AI said Monday that its new campaign, which will initially focus on Kansas, Ohio and Wisconsin, seeks to build support for responsible data center policies and highlight economic opportunities tied to such projects.

The group didn’t specify how much it plans to spend on the campaign but noted it currently has about $50 million in cash on hand.

“The stakes are too high to allow the loudest and most extreme voices to dictate America’s future,” it said in a statement. “Driving responsible investment away will cost Americans good-paying jobs, weaken communities and undermine America’s ability to lead.”

Rob Flaherty, a Democratic strategist and 2024 campaign official for former Vice President Kamala Harris, suggested Build American AI was responding to a recent memo from the National Republican Senatorial Committee (NRSC) warning about data centers’ impact on the Ohio Senate race.

The GOP’s Senate campaign arm called data centers “the anchor hanging around [Sen. Jon] Husted’s neck” and urged AI companies to help fix public perception.

“Sounds like @BuildAmericanAI heeded the call,” Flaherty wrote in a post on X. “NRSC calling in reinforcements.”

Four data center developers separately joined forces Wednesday to launch their own nonprofit, called Infrastructure for America. They aim to focus on “the people who build, power, support, and benefit from data centers.”

The group argued that public discussions about data centers have not reflected “perspectives of the workers who build and operate them, the residents who live in surrounding communities, or the local leaders responsible for making decisions about development and investment.”

However, even as the AI industry puts its messaging efforts in high gear, strategists are skeptical about its immediate impact. Teboe suggested the push was “two years too late.”

“It’s really tough,” Steinhauser added. “It’s tough when public opinion has formed on something to change it, especially something visceral like this … I think it can shift over time, but I don’t see it happening before the election.”

articles.title: Former Air Force secretary: Hegseth’s Pentagon ‘dysfunctional’
articles.summary: Former Secretary of the Air Force Frank Kendall III on Wednesday called the Defense Department under Secretary Pete Hegseth “dysfunctional.” CNN’s Kaitlan Collins asked Kendall, who served under the Biden and Obama administrations, for his assessment of Hegseth’s handling of the military and the Pentagon. The former secretary accused the Pentagon chief of doing “active…
articles.body:
Former Secretary of the Air Force Frank Kendall III on Wednesday called the Defense Department under Secretary Pete Hegseth “dysfunctional.”

CNN’s Kaitlan Collins asked Kendall, who served under the Biden and Obama administrations, for his assessment of Hegseth’s handling of the military and the Pentagon. The former secretary accused the Pentagon chief of doing “active harm” to the department.

“In a word, it’s dysfunctional,” Kendall continued. “I’ve worked with and had a chance to work for maybe a dozen secretaries of Defense. He’s doing active harm to the Department of Defense. It’s not passive. It’s active harm.”

The ex-official said the “enormous damage” to the department will take several years “or decades to go repair this and restore the type of system that we have had traditionally.”

“Right now, in our competition, brain power is just as important as how big somebody’s biceps are,” Kendall added later. “We need people with intellectual capital just as much as we need people who are physically capable. He’s overemphasizing this kind of, you know, ‘bro thing’ with the testosterone thing you mentioned, as well as many other things.”

“That’s not what the secretary of Defense should be worrying about. What he should be worried about is not getting us into a conflict that we have no obvious way out of,” he told Collins, referring to the Iran war as an “absolute disaster.”

Pentagon spokesperson Sean Parnell said in a statement to The Hill that the notion that the Defense Department “is in disarray is completely baseless and an insult to every dedicated professional and warfighter in this building who comes to work every day to defend this nation.”

“This is what reform looks like,” Parnell said. “Leading an enterprise of this scale requires bold leadership, accountability and placing the right personnel in the right places. The department operates on a disciplined ‘next man up mentality and is firing on all cylinders under Secretary Hegseth’s leadership.”

Hegseth has imposed his will on the Pentagon after nearly 20 months in the role of secretary, underlined by the recent resignation of Army Secretary Dan Driscoll. There had been tensions between the two men since they entered their roles last year, but Driscoll praised Hegseth’s support for service members in a post online, breaking his silence about his departure.

“I had the privilege of working with them to modernize and accelerate how the Army mans, trains, and equips the most lethal fighting force on the face of the earth,” he wrote. “We could not have made the progress we did without the support of Secretary Hegseth.”

But Driscoll was displeased with Hegseth’s removal of four Army officers , two women and two Black men, from a one-star general promotion list earlier this year. Hegseth has since removed the names of at least six Army officers from a list for promotions to two-star generals

Hegseth and his allies said the department does not consider gender or skin color when weighing promotions. But his barring of several promotions for officers in both the Navy and Air Force has led other former military leaders to describe the actions as damaging to the service branches.

The secretary is also losing support from Republican lawmakers over the turnover and lack of progress in the Iran war. Sen. Thom Tillis (R-N.C.), a former member of the Senate Armed Services Committee, accused him of “inept management” of the Pentagon and called for President Trump to fire him.

articles.title: DJI’s new robovac can climb obstacles, vacuum quietly, and claims much improved privacy
articles.summary: ﻿Local Data Mode is DJI’s answer to the first Romo’s security crisis.
articles.body: DJI has announced a second generation of its Romo robovac. The Romo 2 series is quieter, more powerful, and better at climbing over small steps and other obstacles. But more importantly for DJI, a new local-only data mode should go some way to reassuring anyone concerned by the first Romo’s serious security flaws. There are actually two new Romo models, the transparent P2 and the opaque A2. Both benefit from improved navigation, apparently able to avoid cables and other obstacles as small as 2mm in size, as well as transparent objects like mirrors or glass. There’s also “human-like reasoning and concept transfer” that supposedly allows Romo 2 to learn from obstacles it’s encountered in the past and adapt to new objects it encounters. [Image: Better at clearing tall obstacles. Two legs on the bottom allow it to climb over single steps up to 4cm (1.5in) in height, or two steps at around double the height. That won’t help it climb a staircase, but it will be able to cross small dividers and thresholds between rooms. On carpet it can reach up to 36,000Pa of suction, while new brush and mop arms have a longer reach for cleaning sideboards and under furniture. DJI says the Romo 2 is much quieter too, with an 85 percent reduction in volume. [Image: [Image: [Image: [Image: [Image: The first Romo is an impressive robot vacuum going by the specs, but that wasn’t enough to overcome huge security flaws which made it possible to access thousands of the robovacs worldwide to expose home floorplans, cameras and microphones, and even full remote control. DJI patched the problems, but by then the reputational damage was done, and we couldn’t quite trust the Romo again. With that in mind, the Romo 2 has a new Local Data Mode, which DJI calls “a new industry standard for home robotics.” It severs the DJI Home’s app connection with the internet, preventing the syncing of photos or camera feeds. Users can also entirely disable the camera and microphone from the vacuum, and delete any stored data. Local Data Mode will roll out to the Romo 2 in Q4 this year, and DJI has plans to expand it to the first line of Romo models too. [Media: The Romo P2 costs a steep €1,299 (around $1,500), while the A2 is €100 cheaper. A US launch is unlikely — US restrictions have prevented DJI from launching any of its recent products in the country, and the FCC’s new ban on foreign-made robot vacuums makes a Romo 2 release even less likely. It was announced at IFA alongside the Osmo 360 II action camera, which is also skipping the US. Update, September 3rd: Added European pricing.

Thom Tillis (R-N.C.), in pushing for the ouster of Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth. “I agree with the sentiments of Sen. Tillis. I hate to tell the president who he should hire and fire. I don’t know if it’s really…
articles.body:
Rep. Don Bacon (R-Neb.) in a Wednesday interview backed up his colleague in the Senate, Sen. Thom Tillis (R-N.C.), in pushing for the ouster of Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth.

“I agree with the sentiments of Sen. Tillis. I hate to tell the president who he should hire and fire. I don’t know if it’s really my role, but I would say this: I would not — he would not be on my team. I think he is — he has not been a very good leader in many ways,” Bacon said of Hegseth on CNN’s “Anderson Cooper 360.”

“So, I agree with the sentiments of Sen. Tillis, and I wouldn’t hire him myself. He would not be on my team,” he added.

Tillis called on President Trump to fire Hegseth over what the North Carolina Republican said was the Defense secretary’s “inept management” of the military.

Tillis ratcheted up his criticism of Hegseth’s leadership in the wake of Army Secretary Dan Driscoll announcing his resignation. Driscoll had butted heads with Hegseth on multiple occasions about the ouster of senior officials.

The North Carolina senator called Driscoll “the right man at the right moment to lead our Soldiers and Army civilians,” while also expressing ire toward Hegseth’s management of his department.

“I have never witnessed more inept management of the brave men and women who serve our country. He is intimidated by competence and retreats to ginning up culture wars instead of soberly attending to the vital work of our national defense and the health and well-being of our fighting force,” Tillis posted on the social platform X.

Key GOP lawmakers have expressed concern about the turnover of senior staff at the Pentagon as well as the lack of a clear plan from the administration to end the war in Iran and the failure of the Trump administration to connect with Democrats to create support for funding priorities.

During his leadership at the Pentagon, Hegseth has been a controversial figure, but increasing tensions between the secretary and top Republicans on Capitol Hill are set to come a head soon, as the administration presses for more than $70 billion in emergency national security spending to cover Iran war costs.

When reached for comment by The Hill, the Pentagon had no comment on Bacon’s remarks.

articles.title: Nvidia acquires Hugging Face in push for open-source technology
articles.summary: The technology giant Nvidia will acquire the open-source platform Hugging Face for nearly $13 billion as part of the company’s push for open artificial intelligence systems. In an announcement Thursday, Nvidia said it will pay $12.93 billion for Hugging Face’s platform, which hosts more than 3 million models and 500,000 datasets used by hundreds of…
articles.body:
The technology giant Nvidia will acquire the open-source platform Hugging Face for nearly $13 billion as part of the company’s push for open artificial intelligence systems.

In an announcement Thursday, Nvidia said it will pay $12.93 billion for Hugging Face’s platform, which hosts more than 3 million models and 500,000 datasets used by hundreds of thousands of other companies.

“Together, we will scale Hugging Face’s platform, strengthen its infrastructure and expand access to AI for developers and institutions worldwide,” Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang wrote in a statement.

Huang said Hugging Face will remain an open platform under the deal.

It comes just more than a month after Nvidia launched its open-source initiative , the Open Secure AI Alliance, for companies to collaborate on open-source tools to identify, patch and disclose security vulnerabilities across infrastructure.

Hugging Face is one of the main collaborators on this project.

“Open models let startups, businesses, universities and public institutions build on advanced capabilities without training every model from scratch,” the announcement said. “They enable organizations to match the right model to the right job.”

Discussions around open-source models ramped up earlier this summer after three AI firms — OpenAI, Anthropic and Meta — revealed their models hacked into other company systems during cybersecurity testing.

Unlike private models hosted by OpenAI and Anthropic, open-source systems are often smaller, less expensive and live in the public domain. This gives virtually anyone or any company access to download and customize the model for a wide range of uses.

Steam picked up in recent months for more open-source development in the U.S., given the rising costs of private, proprietary models like Claude and ChatGPT, and the need to stay ahead of China’s AI development.

Nvidia’s Hugging Face acquisition is the latest in a series of deals for the chipmaker. The company announced last month it is partnering with various Wall Street investment firms to use more than $500 billion in third-party capital for the build-out of AI infrastructure.
