articles.title: Court halts Trump effort to help Congress overturn California clean car rules
articles.summary: A federal judge late Wednesday temporarily blocked a Trump administration effort to overturn California’s clean car rules through Congress. Judge Beryl Howell, an appointee of former President Obama, blocked an Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) move that would have allowed Congress and President Trump to overturn California rules related to vehicle and lawn equipment emissions. In…
articles.body:
A federal judge late Wednesday temporarily blocked a Trump administration effort to overturn California’s clean car rules through Congress.

Judge Beryl Howell, an appointee of former President Obama, blocked an Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) move that would have allowed Congress and President Trump to overturn California rules related to vehicle and lawn equipment emissions.

In years past, the EPA allowed these regulations to move forward by granting waivers that exempted them from the Clean Air Act’s preemption of state laws that are stricter than federal standards.

In June, the agency classified these waivers as “rules, “ an effort to let Congress overturn them using the Congressional Review Act (CRA), which allows lawmaker to nix recently passed rules with simple majority votes and presidential approval.

“The central problem for EPA is that the waivers themselves explicitly state that they are not rules, while the CRA limits invocation of this statute only to agency rules of general applicability, which EPA, in its own words, has emphatically stated Clean Air Act waiver orders are not,” Howell wrote in her ruling.

She said that the agency was trying to get the court to engage in “Orwellian doublethink, offering two explanations simultaneously” for its move.

In her ruling, Howell said that California is likely to ultimately succeed on the merits of the case, and she ordered a return to the status quo prior to the EPA’s June action.

The Hill has reached out to the EPA for comment.

California Attorney General Rob Bonta celebrated the ruling, saying in a statement that “California is taking many steps forward to protect the environment and public health while President Trump is taking six steps back.”

“For 50 years, both Democratic and Republican administrations have upheld California’s authority to enforce state emission standards, but this administration thinks it can roll back the clock and sow chaos even while our lawsuit plays out in court. Today’s decision is a key victory that rebuffs President Trump’s prior efforts. Federal emission standards should be a baseline to protect our future, not a ceiling to limit it,” Bonta said.

Last year, congressional Republicans separately overturned California’s gas-car phaseout using the CRA . That move was challenged in a separate, ongoing case.

articles.title: House Republican: China ‘has it right’ on AI use in classrooms
articles.summary: Rep. Carlos Gimenez (R-Fla.) on Wednesday praised China’s use of artificial intelligence in classrooms. “I think in this case, I think Beijing actually has it right. As long as AI is not used to supplant your ability to learn, in other words, you have to learn the concepts, etc., etc.,” Gimenez told NewsNation’s Blake Burman…
articles.body:
Rep. Carlos Gimenez (R-Fla.) on Wednesday praised China’s use of artificial intelligence in classrooms .

“I think in this case, I think Beijing actually has it right. As long as AI is not used to supplant your ability to learn, in other words, you have to learn the concepts, etc., etc.,” Gimenez told NewsNation’s Blake Burman on “The Hill.”

“What they’re saying is that, ‘At a young age, we’re teaching you what AI is all about and how it can be utilized and how you’ll be conversant, but you’ll be very, very agile with it in the future,’ which will put our children at a disadvantage because like it or not, AI is here,” he added.

In late June, Bloomberg reported that China announced a formal plan for the incorporation of artificial intelligence in every educational level. Per the outlet, China’s State Council had unveiled a blueprint looking five years into the future that featured a plan for AI to become a central skill for all students.

Meanwhile, on Wednesday, New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani (D) announced that the city “will implement a one-year moratorium on generative AI for students in 2-K through 8th grade.”

“The tech industry wants us to believe that AI in early education is not only inevitable, but that it is necessary,” the mayor said at a press conference.

“We do not see it that way. I have yet to see a study showing that AI is beneficial for students in elementary and middle school, with the exception, of course, of research sponsored by the very corporations that stand to profit,” he added.

Last month, Education Secretary Linda McMahon said that AI could be an advantageous tool for students in elementary though high school if schools and teachers use the technology correctly.

articles.title: Former Tiger Woods prosecutor on plea deal: ‘Both sides win’
articles.summary: Dave Aronberg, the former Palm Beach County, Fla., state attorney who prosecuted Tiger Woods in 2017, said Wednesday “both sides win” after the golfer changed his plea to no contest to a recent reckless driving charge. Woods was arrested in March after he struck a pickup truck and flipped his Land Rover in Jupiter, Fla. Aronberg told…
articles.body:
Dave Aronberg, the former Palm Beach County, Fla., state attorney who prosecuted Tiger Woods in 2017, said Wednesday “both sides win” after the golfer changed his plea to no contest to a recent reckless driving charge .

Woods was arrested in March after he struck a pickup truck and flipped his Land Rover in Jupiter, Fla.

Aronberg told NewsNation’s Elizabeth Vargas on “Elizabeth Vargas Reports” that the state’s best evidence against Woods is dashcam footage of his arrest, while Woods’s defense lawyers said the golfer was on prescription drugs for past injuries and “developed a tolerance” and, therefore, was not impaired in this latest crash.

“In this case, both sides win,” Aronberg continued. “It’s not that they’re not throwing out all the charges. He had to pay a price. He had to plead guilty to the lesser offense of reckless driving.”

Aronberg said Woods never blew into a breathalyzer and refused a urinalysis, which left no direct evidence for prosecutors of impairment at the time of the crash, solely relying on the dashcam and body camera video. The video showed Woods appearing disoriented, with two pills found in his pocket.

He noted that State Attorney for the 19th Judicial Circuit Thomas Bakkedahl “did the right thing in that this case is flawed,” referring to Bakkedahl’s defense in accepting the plea change.

“I mean, he didn’t have a slam dunk here,” Aronberg evaluated.

Bakkedahl told reporters Wednesday that he did what he thinks is right.

Woods announced after his arrest that he would step away from golf to seek addiction treatment and commit “to taking the time needed to return in a healthier, stronger and more focused place, both personally and professionally,” he wrote on social media.

His driver’s license will be suspended for five years, as part of his plea agreement, and he will need to pay a fine.

In the 2017 incident, police officers said they had to wake up Woods when they approached his running vehicle before his arrest, ESPN reported citing a police report. The golfer pleaded guilty to the charges and entered a first-offender program.

articles.summary: Moving to a 55+ community can quickly expose your data to scammers and data brokers before you even unpack, putting your whole family at risk.
articles.body: The moving truck hasn't even left the driveway. Somewhere, a scammer may already know three things about you: your name, your new address and something about your age. Maybe not your exact age, but potentially enough information to make you a more attractive target. Federal law sets specific rules for communities that qualify as housing for people 55 and older. One requirement says at least 80% of occupied units must house at least one person who is 55 or older. Those requirements come from the Housing for Older Persons Act. That means an address inside a known 55+ community can give scammers and data brokers another clue about you. Once public records connect your name to that address, data brokers can add it to a much larger profile. That is the part nobody mentions in the moving checklist. One of the study's authors, Julie Brancale, told AARP that residents faced targeting almost immediately after moving in. She said the attempts then continued. A Leisure World resident in Maryland lost close to $800,000 in a gold-bar scam. Meanwhile, one local anti-fraud group estimates that it has recovered roughly $40 million for Florida victims over the years. How retirement community scams can target your family Here's the part that should get your attention. When a scammer searches for information about you, your adult children may appear too. Personal information gives scammers material they can use to make a fraudulent call, text or email sound more believable. However, you can reduce how much additional information someone finds once they start looking. Limit what your community shares First, ask your HOA or community manager whether you can limit or opt out of resident directory listings. Also, ask what information the community shares with other residents. If possible, remove your phone number, email address and photo from community directories. Check what personal information appears online Next, search your name, phone number and new address online to see what appears. articles.summary: The federal government is extending a pause on some construction of President Trump’s signature border wall, as well as additional border construction in a national park in Texas’s Big Bend region, according to court documents. The pause is expected to run though the end of the month. Federal District Judge Jason Pulliam wrote Wednesday that Customs and…
articles.body:
The federal government is extending a pause on some construction of President Trump’s signature border wall, as well as additional border construction in a national park in Texas’s Big Bend region, according to court documents.

The pause is expected to run though the end of the month.

Federal District Judge Jason Pulliam wrote Wednesday that Customs and Border Protection (CBP) informed him that it would “pause all ground disturbing activity for the Big Bend 2 and 4 Projects until September 30, 2026, to allow for additional public engagement.”

On the government’s map of its border construction plans , the Big Bend 4 project appears to be the one that goes through Big Bend National Park, while the Big Bend 2 project is nearby.

Border construction in the region has garnered significant public pushback , including from those who have raised concerns about landowner rights and importance of the national park to the local residents and economy.

CBP had already said it would pause the construction to seek community feedback after the Department of Homeland Security this year waived environmental laws in an effort to expedite the construction.

It also said its work in the park will not include a 30-foot wall.

In the litigation in question, a local resident sued, saying he received a notice that his property would be condemned because of the border construction, blocking his access to the Rio Grande and disrupting his touring business, personal recreation and property value.

Asked to elaborate on the latest extended and public engagement, a spokesperson for the border agency said in a written statement that “CBP Commissioner Rodney Scott met with local stakeholders to discuss efforts related to border security technology in Big Bend National Park.”

“We are working to preserve the landscape and protect the access visitors and local businesses depend on. We are currently evaluating technology options to meet President Trump’s mission of zero illegal border crossings while strengthening the most secure border in American history in highly remote and hard-to-access area,” the spokesperson added.

articles.title: Sanders, Casar call for artificial superintelligence ban amid rogue AI hackings
articles.summary: Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.) and Rep. Greg Casar (D-Texas) are calling for a permanent ban on the development and deployment of artificial superintelligence, citing a series of recent hackings involving “rogue” models. The bicameral duo announced Thursday they will introduce the Ban Artificial Superintelligence Act, which would institute the permanent ban, along with temporarily pausing…
articles.body:
Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.) and Rep. Greg Casar (D-Texas) are calling for a permanent ban on the development and deployment of artificial superintelligence, citing a series of recent hackings involving “rogue” models.

The bicameral duo announced Thursday they will introduce the Ban Artificial Superintelligence Act, which would institute the permanent ban, along with temporarily pausing “advanced AI development” until federal regulators establish safety standards.

The bill would also direct the U.S. to “pursue international agreements to prevent superintelligence from being developed anywhere in the world” and establish a new Cabinet-level federal agency focused on AI safety rules.

Superintelligence refers to AI technologies that will surpass the smartest humans. Several technology leaders, including OpenAI CEO Sam Altman, have suggested superintelligence is on the horizon.

The legislation would also set new penalties for any person or company trying to circumvent the ban, including the corporate death penalty, in which a court forces a company to shut down. Individual developers could also face up to 20 years in prison, the lawmakers said.

The bill is the latest in a series of proposals being floated by progressives in Congress to slow down the development of AI in the wake of the technology’s growing cybersecurity risks.

The lawmakers pointed to recent hacking disclosures from OpenAI, Anthropic and Meta.

OpenAI revealed in July that two of its models breached past an internal testing sandbox and broke into the database of technology firm Hugging Face without any prompt to do so.

Anthropic and Meta later disclosed other incidents in which a misconfiguration by the cybersecurity company Irregular allowed models in isolated environments to access the internet and hack other systems.

“Nearly every day, there is a frightening new story about how Big Tech companies are losing control of the technology they are developing, with potentially cataclysmic results,” Sanders wrote in a press release.

“The leaders of the major AI companies publicly acknowledge that they do not fully understand the technology and that it is escaping their control. It is irresponsible for society to allow them to move forward and make these products even more advanced,” he added.

Casar emphasized AI’s fast development, writing in a statement, “In just four years, we have gone from the first version of ChatGPT to AI models so powerful they cannot be properly controlled.”

articles.title: Fed's Waller channels his inner John Lennon with a plea to 'give disinflation a chance'
articles.summary: By Michael S.
articles.body:
By Michael S. Derby and Howard Schneider

WASHINGTON, Sept 3 (Reuters) - Federal Reserve Governor Christopher Waller said on Thursday he is leaning toward keeping interest rates steady at the U.S. central bank's policy meeting this month if the next batch of inflation data shows price pressures are continuing to moderate.

Pointing to the importance of "what we learn" about inflation data for ‌August, Waller told a Reuters NEXT Newsmaker event in Washington that "if there is continued progress toward our 2% goal, then I am willing to support holding the policy rate at its current level."

"I'm ‌going to paraphrase John Lennon here. Give disinflation a chance" and refrain from prematurely raising rates to allow a cooling process to play out, Waller said. In terms of that patience, "I'm not going to say let's wait until next year, but let's just wait ​and see if we get some improvement on this."

Waller, however, said the data could also move in a way that would lead him to argue that the Fed needs to take action to control price pressures at its September 15-16 policy meeting.

"If inflation comes in hot, I would consider a rate hike," he said.

The Fed governor noted that the central bank's benchmark overnight interest rate, which has been in the 3.50%-3.75% range since December, is "only slightly restricting aggregate demand," and "it may not take much acceleration in inflation to nudge me into supporting tighter policy."

Waller acknowledged that inflation is "meaningfully above" the Fed's 2% target, but said it "is making slow but continued progress on reaching" that ‌level.

He said an easing of inflation, measured by the change over three months ⁠in the Consumer Price Index on an annualized basis, would be the sort of move that would make him comfortable arguing for holding rates steady. He added, however, that he did not want to put a numerical estimate on his threshold for policy action.

The U.S. Labor Department is scheduled next week to release the August CPI ⁠report, which will be the last major data on prices ahead of the next Fed policy meeting. While it is not the central bank's main inflation barometer, Waller said the CPI data will provide "a pretty accurate idea" of where the Personal Consumption Expenditures Price Index will come in.

That index was up 3.7% in July on a year-over-year basis.

Ahead of Waller's remarks, investors had been pricing in solid odds of a quarter-percentage-point rate hike this month. A wide range ​of ​central bank officials has voiced concern about inflation in recent weeks, with some calling for rate hikes and others signaling ​openness to action to bring what have been persistent above-target price pressures back to ‌the target.
authors: By Michael S. Derby and Howard Schneider

articles.title: Jennings: Trump should release ‘formal declaration of victory’ for Iran war
articles.summary: Conservative commentator Scott Jennings said Wednesday that President Trump should issue a “formal declaration of victory” against Iran, as the Trump administration seeks to financially hamper the regime and its allies amid tit-for-tat strikes in the Middle East. Jennings responded to remarks made by fellow CNN political commentator Xochitl Hinojosa on “The Arena with Kasie…
articles.body:
Conservative commentator Scott Jennings said Wednesday that President Trump should issue a “formal declaration of victory” against Iran, as the Trump administration seeks to financially hamper the regime and its allies amid tit-for-tat strikes in the Middle East.

Jennings responded to remarks made by fellow CNN political commentator Xochitl Hinojosa on “The Arena with Kasie Hunt,” when Hinojosa asked what Trump’s exit strategy is . Jennings replied that the exit strategy “is happening right now.”

“It’s the commander in chief’s job, and I’m sure he will do it,” he said. “To explain to the American people how we have won this war. How we are safer and how this is going to benefit the world. That is the next phase of this.”

Jennings then called for an “affirmative, formal declaration of victory,” saying “far be it for me to put a timetable on him.”

“But we’re at the point now where Iran is totally scrambled and defeated, and we need to take credit for it, in my opinion,” he added.

The commentator, who has been floated as a potential successor to former White House press secretary Karoline Leavitt, said the Trump administration’s decision to strike Iran in February was a “righteous” one. He also argued the military operation is “going to work out for the safety and security of the American people,” prompting Hunt to point out the conflict’s massive unpopularity with Americans.

“Voters do not believe that we’ve won this war,” Hinojosa said earlier in the discussion. “They actually don’t even know how we get out of this war. So, if I were a Republican or anybody in a swing district, I would call on the president to come out with a plan to get us out of this war and actually be against the president in terms of, like, claiming victory.”

Trump justified the conflict Tuesday while warning Iran against further strikes on American military bases in Persian Gulf countries. Iran launched missiles and drones toward those allies and bases early the next day in retaliation of renewed U.S. strikes .

The back-and-forth military strikes this week reignited the largest outbreak of fighting after a monthlong stalemate. Both sides have remained stuck over control of the Strait of Hormuz , which Iran has kept closed off to commercial vessels shipping one-fifth of the world’s oil.

The president, who deployed a naval blockade by Iranian ports in the strait, even floated the idea that he could name the body of water after himself, writing on Truth Social that “it would be ‘hotter’ than ever before!”

He has also suggested multiple times since the early days of the conflict that it would come to an end within weeks or months. He repeated this Wednesday as the conflict stretches into its seventh month, telling reporters that he does not “think it will be very much longer” until the conflict ends.

Trump is facing growing pressure to contain the hostilities before the midterms. The White House told Reuters that it would not escalate military action against Iran until after the midterms.

images.caption: CNN contributor Scott Jennings, left, and President Trump.

articles.title: Nick Saban stars in new TV ad advocating for Cruz, Cantwell NCAA bill
articles.summary: Former college football coach Nick Saban is staring in a new advertisement advocating for the Protect College Sports Act, the bipartisan bill that would regulate college sports backed by Sens. Ted Cruz (R-Texas) and Maria Cantwell (D-Wash.) In the ad, set to run during the first week of college football games this weekend, Saban says…
articles.body:
Former college football coach Nick Saban is staring in a new advertisement advocating for the Protect College Sports Act, the bipartisan bill that would regulate college sports backed by Sens. Ted Cruz (R-Texas) and Maria Cantwell (D-Wash.)

In the ad, set to run during the first week of college football games this weekend, Saban says the bill would “end” the “chaos” around issues concerning name, image and likeness endorsement money, and that it also “protects athletes” and women’s sports.

“Join the winning team today and help Congress protect American tradition,” the multi-championship-winning coach says during the 30-second ad .

Saban is one of several major college sports figures who has voiced support for the bill, which would grant the NCAA sweeping antitrust protection and help it better enforce its rules on eligibility, revenue sharing and the transfer portal.

But some critics say the legislation hands the NCAA too much power and would create a system where only top universities benefit from the new rules governing college sports.

Saban spoke to a Senate panel earlier this summer, during which he explained the changes he has seen in college sports during his decades as a coach, conceding the bill being put forth by Cruz and Cantwell “isn’t perfect, and many adjustments need to be made. But this is a serious effort to bring order to a system that badly needs fixing.”

The legislation is expected to face a crucial vote in the Senate when lawmakers return from August recess later this month.

articles.title: Microsoft backing measure protecting consumers over data center water usage costs
articles.summary: Microsoft is throwing its support behind legislation that would prevent data centers from passing along water usage costs to consumers, as tech companies seek to allay community concerns about the AI infrastructure. The Water Cost Accountability Act would direct states to block public water systems from recovering costs associated with connecting data centers from anyone…
articles.body:
Microsoft is throwing its support behind legislation that would prevent data centers from passing along water usage costs to consumers, as tech companies seek to allay community concerns about the AI infrastructure.

The Water Cost Accountability Act would direct states to block public water systems from recovering costs associated with connecting data centers from anyone other than their developers or owners.

“This legislation represents an important step toward building the infrastructure needed for America’s future while strengthening trust with the communities that host it,” said Fred Humphries, corporate vice president of U.S. government affairs at Microsoft, in a statement.

“It also reinforces the principle that companies must responsibly show up in communities across the country, engaging as long-term partners and listening to local voices,” he continued.

Local communities have increasingly pushed back on new data center projects over concerns about the impact on water usage and electricity costs, as well as potential noise and environmental pollution.

The server warehouses used about 66 billion liters of water in 2023, according to Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory. As of 2015, the U.S. used about 322 billion gallons per day, or more than 400 trillion liters per year, with power plants and irrigation accounting for the greatest usage.

AI companies and data center developers have argued the concerns over water usage are overblown and have pointed to technology that can reduce their reliance on water for cooling in newer construction.

Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick also pushed back on the issue Wednesday, suggesting it is “propaganda by our adversaries to try to slow us down.”

“One of my favorite things is when people talk about data centers using water. The No. 1 product in America that uses water is cattle,” he told CNBC, adding, “I mean, data centers don’t use water.”

However, Republican lawmakers appear keen to alleviate their constituents’ concerns as data centers become a key issue in the upcoming midterm elections.

“They [data centers] are major drivers of investment, economic growth, job creation, the development of our nation’s digital infrastructure,” said Rep. Gary Palmer (R-Ala.), who chairs the House Energy and Commerce Subcommittee on Environment, at a hearing Thursday.

“However, those benefits should not come at the expense of families and small businesses through higher water rates,” he added.

articles.title: FAA proposes permanent flight restrictions over Mar-a-Lago
articles.summary: The Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) proposed a new rule Wednesday that would place permanent restrictions on what flights are permitted within a one-mile radius of Mar-a-Lago. The proposed rule would “establish a flight restriction from the surface to 2,000 feet” above mean sea level “within a one NM radius of Mar-a-Lago Club.” These were temporary…
articles.body:
The Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) proposed a new rule Wednesday that would place permanent restrictions on what flights are permitted within a one-mile radius of Mar-a-Lago .

The proposed rule would “establish a flight restriction from the surface to 2,000 feet” above mean sea level “within a one NM radius of Mar-a-Lago Club.” These were temporary restrictions in Oct. 2025 amid heightened security concerns that the FAA now wants to make permanent.

“Aircraft would essentially be unable to use Runway 28R/10L,” the FAA wrote.

The runway is one of three available at President Donald J. Trump International Airport — formerly Palm Beach International Airport — but remains the airport’s main commercial runway.

Runway 28R/10L reportedly handled 86 flights a day in 2025.

The FAA will be accepting public comments through Oct. 2.

The agency has already enforced similar requests by the Secret Service to divert planes over Mar-a-Lago since the start of Trump’s second term, but residents of Palm Beach County complained at the time about the diversions.

“My house is filled with the smell of jet fuel,” Jane Jones, a resident of Palm Beach, told the county’s Citizens Committee during a 2025 hearing about the redirected planes.

Other residents complained about the possible health effects this could have on locals and what one person said was a “double-digit decrease in your property value.”

“Our white roof was white — it is now gray,” said a West Palm Beach resident. “Given the current circumstances, it will eventually get black.”

A 2020 study from the University of Washington reported “airport operations result in noise and air pollution, which are linked to many of the health outcomes experienced by airport communities.”

It added that evidence “found lower life expectancy and increased risk of various health problems, from stroke to heart disease to respiratory problems” for individuals living near airports.

Palm Beach County filed a lawsuit with a federal court over these restrictions, arguing similar claims from the residents at the 2025 hearing.

“Residents reported: being disturbed by aircraft noise as early as 6:00 a.m. and as late as 11:00 p.m.; an inability to converse outside due to aircraft noise; soot covering their properties; the smell of jet fuel permeating their homes; potential damage to the architectural features of historic homes,” the lawsuit said.

The pending lawsuit also claimed the FAA failed to follow proper procedures when instituting the initial no-fly zone over Mar-a-Lago — including a National Environmental Policy Act environmental review.

articles.title: Bipartisan insulin price cap introduced in House as lawmakers seek affordability win
articles.summary: Bipartisan House lawmakers, including two battleground Republicans, introduced legislation Thursday to ensure people with private health insurance don’t pay more than $35 a month for insulin. Lawmakers have discussed the idea of an insulin cap for years but haven’t been able to get legislation over the finish line over GOP resistance to government setting prices.…
articles.body:
Bipartisan House lawmakers, including two battleground Republicans, introduced legislation Thursday to ensure people with private health insurance don’t pay more than $35 a month for insulin.

Lawmakers have discussed the idea of an insulin cap for years but haven’t been able to get legislation over the finish line over GOP resistance to government setting prices.

But two Republicans in contested battleground districts signing on shows that the GOP is trying to address concerns about the cost of healthcare ahead of the midterm elections.

The Insulin Act — shorthand for the Improving Needed Safeguards for Users of Lifesaving Insulin Now Act — was introduced by Reps. Diana DeGette (D-Colo.), Angie Craig (D-Minn.), Kim Schrier (D-Wash.), Mariannette Miller-Meeks (R-Iowa) and Rob Bresnahan (R-Pa.).

It’s a companion version of legislation that advanced through the Senate Health Committee earlier this summer . That bill is being pushed by Sens. Susan Collins (R-Maine), Jeanne Shaheen (D-N.H.), Raphael Warnock (D-Ga.) and John Kennedy (R-La.). In total, it has 28 co-sponsors divided equally between the parties.

Aside from capping out-of-pocket costs at $35, the House bill would prohibit healthcare plans from applying any deductible to select insulin products, expedite the development and review of biosimilar insulin, and establish a hotline and resource center to help uninsured people get access to insulin.

Insulin has long been targeted by lawmakers as an example of the broken incentives in the U.S. health system. The drug hasn’t changed much since it was first discovered more than 100 years ago, and as newer forms of the drug have been introduced, the price has climbed. An estimated 40 million Americans are living with diabetes.

A key measure in former President Biden’s 2022 Inflation Reduction Act capped insulin prices to $35 per month for seniors on Medicare. That measure passed without any GOP support.

Since then, many pharmaceutical companies have voluntarily reduced their prices.

The House in 2022 passed a Democratic-sponsored insulin pricing bill for both private insurers and Medicare on a largely party-line vote . Miller-Meeks, a physician, was one of only 12 Republicans to vote in favor of it.

At the time, Republicans accused Democrats of “socialist price controls” that would allow pharmacy benefit managers to hide savings from patients.

Despite the bipartisan support, the Senate version has yet to make it to the floor. Concerns over the cost of the bill may keep some Republicans away, though supporters hope that the House introduction will add momentum.

With limited time before the midterms — the House is in session just one more week — the best chance for passage could be during the lame-duck period as part of a year-end spending bill.

articles.title: Interior preparing to start work on Trump’s arch ‘over the next two-week period’
articles.summary: The federal government is preparing “over the next two weeks” to start work on President Trump’s proposed triumphal arch in the Washington, D.C. area, Interior Secretary Doug Burgum said Thursday. “We are preparing to start, over the next two-week period, the excavation work necessary for the Great Triumphal Arch and Military Observation Deck,” Burgum said…
articles.body:
The federal government is preparing “over the next two weeks” to start work on President Trump’s proposed triumphal arch in the Washington, D.C. area, Interior Secretary Doug Burgum said Thursday.

“We are preparing to start, over the next two-week period, the excavation work necessary for the Great Triumphal Arch and Military Observation Deck,” Burgum said in a post on X.

It was not entirely clear from Burgum’s post whether excavation work itself was starting in two weeks or if the department was simply preparing for that work to start.

The Hill has reached out to Interior for clarification.

In his post, Burgum said that he arch will be “one of the Great Pieces of American Architecture, honoring the history and significance of Arlington Cemetery and befitting the most powerful Capital in the World.”

The arch is one of several D.C.-based projects that the president has championed. Trump said earlier this year that he’d like for it to be the biggest in the world.

A federal assessment recently said that the arch would adversely impact dozens of historic sites around the city, including by obstructing views.

articles.title: OpenAI releases new model after reaching ‘critical’ cyber threshold
articles.summary: OpenAI began rolling out its latest AI model, GPT-6 Astra, to a limited group of organizations Thursday, after declaring earlier this week that it was the first model to cross the company’s threshold for heightened cyber capabilities. The ChatGPT maker said the model will become available to more paid users in the coming days. “GPT‑6…
articles.body:
OpenAI began rolling out its latest AI model, GPT-6 Astra, to a limited group of organizations Thursday, after declaring earlier this week that it was the first model to cross the company’s threshold for heightened cyber capabilities.

The ChatGPT maker said the model will become available to more paid users in the coming days.

“GPT‑6 Astra brings together years of research and big bets across pre-training, reinforcement learning, and alignment,” the company said. “Astra is state-of-the-art on computer use, browsing, software engineering, cybersecurity, science, and professional work.”

OpenAI hinted at the release Tuesday, explaining that Astra was the first model to reach its threshold for “critical” cyber capabilities. This means it can find and exploit unknown security flaws in well-protected systems without human involvement.

The company said it delayed parts of the model’s development and release to strengthen protections, which it believes “sufficiently minimize the risk of severe harm.”

The version of Astra being rolled out Thursday includes limits on more advanced cyber tasks, it noted. However, some cyberdefenders will gain access to an iteration with less restrictive safeguards in the coming weeks through its Daybreak initiative.

Astra’s release comes as the AI industry grapples with the increasing capabilities and risks from new models. In July, AI agents from OpenAI escaped their testing environment and hacked into the tech startup Hugging Face .

The incident, which provoked fears about uncontrolled AI in both Silicon Valley and Washington, was quickly followed by several other reports of agents improperly gaining access to the internet and hacking into other companies.

OpenAI suggested Thursday that Astra is its “most aligned model, with substantial improvements in understanding user intent and model behavior—you can delegate tasks with greater confidence in Astra’s judgment.”

The company said it built a new evaluation based on the Hugging Face incident to test whether a model will go outside its intended scope to accomplish a difficult task.
